lesson.subtitle: Lesson 5 -- Your Personal Statement
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Gabriel Fernandes | Lesson 5 -- Your Personal Statement

listenings.text: I read about nine hundred of these a year, and the ones I remember are never the ones about the biggest thing that happened to somebody. They are the ones about the smallest thing, told properly. Somebody wrote to me once about the week a market stall lost money, and I still remember the number of unsold boxes. That is what a vivid detail does. What almost everybody gets wrong is the second half. They tell me the story and then they stop, or they end with a sentence that could belong to anybody: this taught me the value of hard work. That is a cliche, and it tells me nothing. I want the insight that only you could have had, and I want to hear that you are still carrying it.

My first draft was about everything I had ever done, and it was terrible. My teacher read it and asked me one question: which of these do you still think about? I narrowed it down to one Saturday. The fourth draft was about that Saturday and nothing else, and it was half the length. The part I found hardest was not the writing. It was that I had to say what I had understood, in the present, and I kept slipping back into the past because the story was in the past. I read the whole thing out loud to my mother, twice, and both times I caught something my eyes had walked straight over.

extra_audio.text: You narrow down from everything you have done to one thing that actually changed you. You write the anecdote in the past, in as much detail as you can remember. You say what you have understood since, and that part is in the present perfect. You cut every sentence that could belong to somebody else. You read it out loud and you proofread it once more before you send it.
